title: Behavioral and Neurobiological Outcomes in the Reserpine-Induced Fibromyalgia-Like Model in Rodents: A Scoping Review
content: Background: Fibromyalgia (FM) is a chronic nociplastic pain condition characterized by widespread pain and non-nociceptive symptoms. The reserpine-induced model is widely used to investigate FM-like phenotypes in rodents, but methodological heterogeneity may affect phenotype expression and reproducibility. Objective: This scoping review intended to identify published research that involved behavioral and neurobiological outcomes of reserpine-induced FM-like conditions and identify factors underlying phenotypic varia-bility. Design: Four databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus) were as-sessed. The search strategy was not restricted by publication date. Eligible studies were experimental studies in rats or mice using reserpine-based protocols and reporting affec-tive, cognitive, or neurobiological outcomes. Study selection and data extraction were in-dependently performed by two reviewers, and methodological quality was assessed using SYRCLE. Results: This review shows that a study heterogeneity is further increased by species, strain, sex, reserpine dose and administration regimen, vehicle composition, out-come assessment timing, and experimental settings. Thus, these aspects should be ad-dressed while interpreting and comparing test data. In rodent research, the most consist-ently observed characteristic is the emergence of long-term mechanical and deep-tissue hypersensitivity, accompanied by converging alterations in monoaminergic modulation, neuroimmune and inflammatory signaling, spinal and supraspinal excitability, and pe-ripheral metabolic and oxidative functions. This alignment of behavioral, neurochemical, electrophysiological, histological, and peripheral results offers biological validity to the paradigm, expanding outside simply inducing nociceptive hypersensitivity. Conclusions: Using reserpine to evaluate fibromyalgia-associated pain biology is useful and mechanis-tically relevant. Behavioral, neurochemical, electrophysiological, histological, and periph-eral data support the paradigm beyond nociceptive hypersensitivity.
